In this episode of Across Acoustics, the podcast of ASA Publications, Miski Mohamed and Matthew Winn discuss their JASA paper “Acoustic analysis of Taylor Swift’s dialect changes across different eras of her career.” Studies usually compare dialect groups; following one person’s speech over the years is much harder. Swift is an ideal exception: she moved between places and social worlds, often with clear goals, and she has been recorded in interviews constantly. A similar long-term study once showed Queen Elizabeth II’s Christmas broadcasts drifting from an upper-class accent toward a more mainstream one.

The researchers analyzed speech, not singing, because accompaniment makes sung vowels hard to measure. Using clean interview recordings from her Philadelphia, Nashville and New York periods, they measured dozens of vowels per time point, excluding those next to nasal consonants, and used Praat scripts to estimate the first two formants at ten points in each vowel.

In Nashville, immersed in the Southern-accented country scene, Swift adopted Southern features: the diphthong in “ride” flattened toward “rad,” and the vowel in “who” moved forward toward “hew.” In her New York era (2019), as she began speaking out on social change, feminism and artists’ rights, her median pitch fell from 197 Hz to 182 Hz, a shift the authors attribute to social rather than age-related factors. Her Philadelphia roots still show in the backed vowel of “school” and “cool.” Re-recorded albums, by contrast, proved remarkably consistent with the originals.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from the Across Acoustics episode “The Eras of Taylor Swift’s Changing Dialect,” with Miski Mohamed and Matthew Winn (ASA Publications, 2025). Listen to the podcast.
